After Trump was elected president of the United States, the global economy faced greater uncertainty. After the new US government took office, the direction of US policy may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects—from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to anti-globalization—which may have profound implications for the global economic landscape. It is worth noting that the accelerated pace of interest rate hikes in the US, the strengthened dollar, and the possibility of the US taking trade protectionist measures have exacerbated the risks faced by emerging market economies. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained relatively stable, while Hong Kong banks' interbank lending rates have risen along with dollar interbank lending rates. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remain good, and overall loan growth further increased in the second half of 2016. Following the implementation of the new stamp duty measures, the residential property market immediately showed signs of adjustment, but has recently rebounded. Looking ahead, banks should cautiously assess the possibility that the pace of interest rate hikes in the US may be faster than expected, as well as the impact of broader US policy uncertainty, particularly the risk of large-scale capital outflows and the potential effect on Hong Kong interest rates. After Trump was elected president of the US, the global economy faced greater uncertainty. Not only did the election results surprise the market, but the related market reaction was also unexpected. In particular, expectations that measures such as the tax reform introduced by Trump, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation will drive US economic growth are propelling the global stock market upward. After the new US government took office, the direction of US policy may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects—from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to anti-globalization—or will have profound implications for the global economic landscape. However, the expected tax cuts by Trump may fail to generate the anticipated stimulus to US economic growth in the market. Especially as current US economic activities are approaching their potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only bring a mild cyclical stimulus effect to US economic growth, but will exacerbate the upward risk of US inflation. Although it remains unknown whether the US Federal Reserve will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening because of this, long-term bond yields have clearly risen, partially reflecting market expectations that inflation risk is increasing. At the same time, the rise of trade protectionism will cause a "double loss" for the US and other regions worldwide. Increased trade barriers will lead to market distortion and harm overall interests, impede global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and bring downside risks to the global economic outlook. At the same time, unstable geopolitical conditions remain a major risk and adverse factor, especially for the European economy, which is still weak in its recovery. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflow has increased due to the accelerating pace of US interest rate hikes and the further appreciation of the dollar. This may drag down economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid capital outflow. In fact, anticipating that the Trump administration will implement large-scale fiscal expansion and concerns over surging energy prices, the market has repriced the inflation risk, leading to a comprehensive and significant rise in long-term bond yields across developed economies and several emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 (see page 13) assess the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hikes on the sovereign bond market of 26 selected economies. Research results indicate that since the "reduce buying panic" in 2013, the impact of the US Treasury bond market on the sovereign bond market has deepened, and US interest rate hikes and tighter financial conditions will have a significant impact on developed economies and emerging market economies. In East Asia, with the rebound in exports, economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016, but market fluctuations such as currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields in the region, which were previously caused by concerns about potential policy changes by the new US government, gradually stabilized by the early part of this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain stable growth in 2017, but the risks and uncertainties it faces are also increasing. US interest rate hikes, currency depreciation in the region, and increased volatility in the financial market may lead to a tightening of financial conditions. At the same time, the US may implement protectionist policies, which may affect the regional economy, but the actual impact is not yet clear. In China, the overall economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016, driven by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private sector spending. Although the economy continues to show signs of stabilization, the growth prospects in China remain uncertain. Especially in the situation where the government is determined to curb housing price increases, if the real estate market continues to cool down, the contribution of the real estate industry to growth this year may decrease. At the same time, the continued progression of economic structural adjustments and the changes in the China-US trade relationship may increase short-term economic uncertainty. Externally, although the RMB remained stable against a basket of currencies at the China Foreign Exchange Trade Center (CFETS) during the reporting period, the pressure of capital outflow increased by the end of 2016 due to the appreciation of the dollar and interest rate hikes in the US, and subsequently seemed to slightly ease in early 2017. Although there are signs of stabilization in private sector economic activities, there are still some concerns in the market regarding the effectiveness of monetary policy, especially given that M1 growth is accelerating while M2 growth is slowing down. Special Topic 2 (see page 24) explores the question of whether the China economy is trapped in a liquidity trap, and Special Topic 3 (see page 27) investigates the factors that may lead to a divergence between M1 and M2 growth. Research results indicate there is no evidence that China has fallen into a liquidity trap, and the main reasons why M1 growth has significantly outpaced M2 are the reduced opportunity cost of holding liquid currency due to recent monetary easing, and the increased economic uncertainty which may have augmented precautionary demand for money. Hong Kong's economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016. Quarterly real local GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Locally, private consumption continues to strengthen, and the robust infrastructure activities in the fourth quarter drove investment growth. Externally, the growth in goods exports increased with the improvement in intra-regional trade flows, while services exports grew steadily with the recovery of trade-related and transportation services. Due to the faster growth in imports of goods and services, net exports will continue to drag down the growth of real local GDP in the second half of the year. With the rise in economic growth, the overall unemployment rate slightly decreased to 3.3% in December. The economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. The consensus between the government and the market for the growth of real local GDP in 2017 is 2-3% and 2.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth prospects still face significant external headwinds. The protectionist tone of the new US government increases the downside risks facing global trade and external demand in Hong Kong. Facing pressure from the appreciation of the dollar and the accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to reduce support for the real economy, and in the event of tail risks emerging, this may lead to tighter local financial conditions. Special Topic 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of the Hong Kong financial conditions index to assist in the supervision of local financial conditions. Since the second half of 2016, local inflation pressure has remained moderate, while the quarterly inflation momentum slightly accelerated in the fourth quarter, mainly due to fluctuations in food prices and rising housing rents. Due to stable import prices, local cost pressure is mild, and expected inflation pressure remains controllable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained relatively stable, but it weakened somewhat after the US interest rate hikes in December. The redemption guarantee has not been triggered. As the dollar appreciates, the nominal exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar further rises. Due to the large currency base, interbank lending rates in Hong Kong banks remain low, but they have risen since October due to year-end funding demands and the recovery of dollar interest rate hikes. Therefore, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October due to intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average mortgage interest rate slightly increased to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, while growth in the first half was 2.2%. Growth is supported by the strengthened local economic activities and the increased financing needs of multinational corporations at year-end. Domestic loan growth slightly accelerated, while overseas loan usage in Hong Kong decreased slightly in the first half before recovering. According to currency analysis, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans recorded a 3.2% increase as borrowers in China gradually reduced repayments of foreign currency loans. The financial condition of the banks remains generally stable. The Hong Kong dollar credit ratio slightly fell to 77.1% at year-end 2016, reflecting that credit growth exceeded loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio decreased to 59.9% by year-end, and the dollar loan-to-deposit ratio significantly fell to 63.8% due to strong growth in dollar credit. Due to the strength of the dollar, both onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates have weakened. In this context, the offshore RMB fund pool in Hong Kong (including customer credit and certificate of deposit balances) is further solidifying with other offshore RMB markets, and the volatility of interbank lending rates for Hong Kong banks has significantly increased. Nevertheless, the liquidity management of RMB by the banks remains stable, and the average daily transaction amount in the RMB real-time payment settlement system remains at a high level. The offshore RMB business in Hong Kong will likely continue to face resistance from the uncertainty in the RMB exchange rate trend. With the improvement in global market conditions, the Hong Kong Stock market experienced significant gains during the reporting period. Although the election of the president of the United States yielded unexpected results, the market only experienced a brief shock. This is mainly due to investors' anticipation of the fiscal stimulus measures of the Trump administration government, driving the global market upward. Although benefiting from this, the Hong Kong market has also shown prudence alongside optimism, the reasons possibly being concerns about the acceleration of US interest rate hikes, challenges facing the China economy, unclear RMB policy, and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the Hong Kong market may be affected by external economic conditions, its valuation attractiveness can provide support to the market. Although the Hong Kong dollar bond yield rapidly increased at year-end and the spread with US Treasury bonds rapidly widened, the Hong Kong dollar bond market continued to expand steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, the offshore RMB bond market in Hong Kong recovered in the second half after contracting in the first half of 2016, but the total issuance of new bonds for the full year was still lower than the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their investment strategies that previously sought returns, both the Hong Kong dollar and the offshore RMB bond market will face pressure. Due to the lack of clarity in US trade policy, the RMB exchange rate may still fluctuate, and the outlook for both bond markets will continue to be troubled by significant uncertainties over the next six months. Following the government's introduction of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market immediately showed signs of adjustment, but has recently rebounded. Given the renewed exuberance in the market, the government will raise the stamp duty to 15% in November. Trading volume in the primary and secondary market has declined in the last two months. However, trading volume has increased recently, partly reflecting developers increasing the launch of primary properties. Meanwhile, property prices continue to reach new highs, but the upward momentum has slowed.

After Trump's unexpected victory as president of the United States, the uncertainty of U.S. policy increased. Although market focus is concentrated on the short-term benefits brought by potential large-scale fiscal policies and business facilitation measures, the current U.S. economic activities are approaching their potential, and fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical stimulus effect to U.S. economic growth, but will further exacerbate the upward risk of inflation. More importantly, the risks faced by emerging market economies are increasing due to the pressure of capital outflows brought about by the acceleration of U.S. interest rate hikes and the strengthening of the dollar, and U.S. potential trade protectionist measures will also threaten global trade. In the East Asian region, real economic activities slightly improved in the second half of 2016, and export volume has also increased recently. However, against the backdrop of interest rate hikes in the U.S., the appreciation of the dollar, and potential protectionist measures by the U.S., financial markets are expected to continue to fluctuate, and the downside risk to economic growth is increasing. In China, the overall economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016, driven by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private sector spending. The domestic economy continues to undergo rebalancing, the tertiary industry is steadily expanding, but the continued progression of economic structural adjustments and the changes in China-US trade relations may increase short-term economic uncertainty. In the situation where the government is determined to curb housing price increases, if the real estate market continues to cool down, the contribution of the real estate industry to economic growth this year may also decrease. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against a basket of currencies at the China Foreign Exchange Trade Center (CFETS) during the reporting period, capital outflow pressure increased at the end of 2016 due to the appreciation of the dollar and interest rate hikes by the U.S., and subsequently seemed to slightly ease in early 2017. After Trump's unexpected victory as president of the United States, the global financial markets reacted strongly, especially as the market anticipated that Trump's implementation of tax reforms, large-scale infrastructure spending, and deregulation would boost U.S. economic growth and inflation, providing a stimulus that spurred the rise in major stock markets (Figure 2.1). Therefore, market expectations for inflation in the U.S. and U.S. interest rate hikes have risen, causing U.S. Treasury bond yields to surge and the dollar to strengthen. Figure 2.1: The stock market indices of some advanced economies; however, the market expectation is that Trump's tax cuts may not have the positive impact on U.S. economic growth that is expected by the market. Although economic policy shifting to rely on fiscal easing measures will help alleviate the heavy burden of monetary easing policies, given the current stage of the U.S. economic cycle, the appropriateness of implementing fiscal easing measures at this time is debatable. Although the growth rate of the U.S. economy has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap is gradually narrowing, and the unemployment rate in February also met the Federal Reserve's estimate of the 4.7% natural rate of unemployment, reflecting that U.S. economic activities are approaching their potential. The U.S. economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, and the fiscal multiplier will be lower than during a recession (for example, please refer to Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012)) 1. In fact, recent estimates of the U.S. Laffer curve indicate that tax cuts in terms of labor or capital may lead to a decrease in tax revenue (for example, please refer to Trabandt and Uhlig (2012)). Regardless, in a situation of reduced excess capacity, any further measures to promote economic growth, even if the substantive impact on economic growth is limited, may increase inflation. Concurrently, rising oil and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionist measures, including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, may exacerbate the upward risk of inflation in the U.S. Even though the risk of rising inflation in the U.S. increases, the Federal Reserve remains cautious about tightening U.S. monetary policy and tends to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partially reflecting increased inflation risk in the U.S. Since the U.S. election, although market forecasts for future federal funds rates have been raised to near the median of the Federal Reserve's forecast for early 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Federal Reserve's long-term forecast (Figure 2.2). Therefore, the acceleration of interest rate hikes in the U.S. may trigger the risk of significant market volatility. Although the focus of the financial markets is concentrated on the short-term benefits brought about by potential expansionary fiscal policies and business facilitation measures driving stronger growth in the U.S. economy, long-term risks still exist, including detrimental protectionist trade policies and further increases in U.S. national debt. In fact, the Trump government may fulfill its election promises by taking trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers will lead to market distortion and harm overall interests, impede global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and bring downside risks to the global economic outlook. Figure 2.2 Future Federal Funds Rate Forecast: For the Federal Reserve and the Europe market, political instability remains the main risk and obstacle to European economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the Eurozone is gradually improving, real gross domestic product in the fourth quarter grew by 1.7% year-on-year, slightly lower than the 1.8% growth in the third quarter; however, compared to the stronger recovery of the U.S. economy, Eurozone economic activities remain only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels (Figure 2.3). Since the decision to leave the UK last summer, the market has been concerned that the Eurozone will ultimately disintegrate. Although Italy's economic and geopolitical situation appears to have stabilized after forming a new government and implementing measures to save the banks, the elections or meetings that Germany and France (possibly including Italy) are about to hold, against the backdrop of the UK Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment, will become a political flashpoint. Due to increased geopolitical uncertainty, sovereign bond yields in Europe continue to climb, and corporate bond spreads are also widening. This situation is particularly evident in neighboring countries and could create a vicious cycle for the real economy, potentially putting pressure on commercial real investment in the Eurozone. Figure 2.3 Real Gross Domestic Product of major advanced economies: Japan's real gross domestic product has improved over the past few quarters, with the year-on-year growth rate for the fourth quarter of 2016 reaching 1.6%, the fastest growth since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger economic recovery than previously anticipated. However, some due to structural problems in the labor market, causing slow wage growth, led to weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the Japanese yen has recently depreciated rapidly, meaning the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation caused by the earlier yen appreciation is about to begin to fade. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery momentum, this indicates an improvement in the short-term inflation outlook, and although "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) fell to 0.1% in December, it is expected to bottom out and recover. Nevertheless, facing long-term and structural headwinds, growth may still be slow, and inflation expectations remain around 0.5% – 0.6%, lower than the level when the Bank of Japan launched its monetary easing in early 2014, thus the risk that the inflation rate will not reach the Bank of Japan's medium-term target of 2% still exists. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits of faster economic growth through trade channels resulting from reduced imports by the U.S. after the global financial crisis, and the possibility that the U.S. may implement protectionist policies, may be smaller. Meanwhile, the acceleration of interest rate hikes in the U.S. and the further appreciation of the dollar will lead to tighter financial conditions and exacerbate economic downside risks. This may drag down economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflow. In fact, market expectations that the Trump government will implement large-scale fiscal expansion, coupled with concerns over surging energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risk, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across developed economies and even several emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 assess the potential spillover effects of U.S. interest rate hikes on the sovereign bond market of 26 selected economies. In the East Asian region, the real economy activities have recently recovered vitality, and the local gross domestic product in the area has grown slightly, while inflation has risen. Real local gross domestic product growth — in the second half of 2016, due to stable private consumption in multiple district economies, economic growth generally remained stable. Meanwhile, exports generally rose slightly from the low levels of 2015. This benefits not only from the stabilization of China's growth but also from the improved performance of developed economies such as the U.S. and Europe. For commodity net exporters (such as Malaysia and Indonesia), a rise in commodity prices also has an additional driving effect. Other major exporting countries (such as South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) are also regaining momentum due to the growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — With the rise in commodity prices (especially oil), producer price inflation is generally on the rise. Although this will increase industrial costs or consumption expenditure, consumption and investment growth may increase due to a decrease in the risk of long-term deflation. Accelerated producer price inflation or will exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which the increase in producer prices is passed on to consumption prices, and this is not uniform across different economies. Consensus forecasts for the consumption price index indicate that inflation in several economies within the region will still be slightly below the 2017 inflation targets of each central bank, but will rise to a level closer to the target (Figure 2.4). Excluding Indonesia, central banks in the East Asian region generally maintained their accommodative monetary policies, while Indonesia cut interest rates twice in September and October of last year to stimulate growth. Figure 2.4: Despite improvements in the real economy, the results of the president of the United States election in November 2016 were unexpected, leading to short-term volatility in the financial markets for the inflation, forecast, and central bank target of the consumption price index in the East Asian region. Foreign exchange market — after the president of the United States election, investors anticipate an increase in U.S. inflation, and most currencies in the region will depreciate against the dollar. However, by trade weighted measure, some currencies in the region depreciated less after the U.S. election, or even slightly appreciated (Figure 2.5). Figure 2.5 Changes in Bond Market and Market Following the Depreciation of the Dollar and Nominal Effective Exchange Rate After the U.S. Election — Asset prices temporarily declined after the president of the United States election but subsequently stabilized. The spread between sovereign bonds of East Asian region economies and U.S. Treasury bonds is rising. However, as the market stabilized, the yields of some regional economies declined, but have not yet recovered to pre-election levels. (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, the interest rate spread has narrowed compared to the pre-election level. (Figure 2.6) Flow of securities investment towards 10-year sovereign bonds and U.S. Treasury bonds—securities investment funds flowed out of the East Asian region in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "cut buying panic" period in mid-2013. Until the initial few weeks in 2017, capital inflows were recorded again, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, growth within the region is expected to remain stable, but the pace is still lower than the historical average. Due to the increased uncertainty in U.S. government policy and the uncertainty regarding the policy response that the Federal Reserve may make, the financial markets are likely to remain volatile. The dollar and yield have risen significantly, which may attract capital to flow from within the region to the U.S., leading investors to reduce their investment in assets within the region, which is particularly worrying for assets whose current valuations are already high. Tightening of financial conditions in this situation will also cause enterprises with substantial debt denominated in dollar to face repayment pressure. Macroeconomically, the global universal interest rate hikes will also lead to a decrease in fixed capital investment within the region, which will not only drag down aggregate demand in the short term but may also affect potential growth in the long term. Finally, exporting countries within the region face the potential threat of new trade protectionist policies implemented by the U.S. government. The trade deficit between the U.S. and East Asian economies has continued to expand in recent years (Figure 2.7), particularly in major export industries within the region, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, apparel, and textiles. In the past decades-high, the U.S. has seen an increase in imports in these industries and a significant loss of employment positions. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalizing U.S. manufacturing may pose a significant risk to exporting countries within the region.

Private consumption growth accelerated and public sector building and construction activities boomed, driving a slight acceleration in Hong Kong's economic growth in the second half of 2016. Due to the increasing uncertainty of the external environment, the economic growth for 2017 is expected to be moderate. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflation pressure is expected to remain under control. Hong Kong's economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016. Real Gross Domestic Product, adjusted for seasonal factors, grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate in the third quarter (Figure 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and a stable labor market situation, the rate of private consumption growth has accelerated, becoming the main driver of Gross Domestic Product growth. With the support of infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong International Airport, building and construction activities have also become prosperous. However, due to weak corporate capital expenditure, the contribution of overall investment expenditure to Gross Domestic Product growth has narrowed. Externally, the import and export of goods are accelerating in growth in line with the rise in intra-regional trade (Figure 3.2). Services related to trade and transportation are driving further growth in service exports, while service imports are rebounding partly due to strong tourism demand from local residents. Net exports continue to drag down Gross Domestic Product growth. Figure 3.1 Growth rate of Real Gross Domestic Product and contribution of major expenditure components. Figure 3.2 Real trade and labor market remain tight. The unemployment rate, adjusted for seasonal factors, remained at 3.4% in the first three quarters, and slightly decreased to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Figure 3.3). In fact, the unemployment rates in several major industries have all decreased in the second half of the year, including the retail, accommodation, and food service sectors, partly due to the stabilization of the retail sector's slowdown. The total number of employed persons reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labor force participation rate remained stable at approximately 61%. Figure 3.3: The unemployment rate and total employment numbers indicate that real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. Regarding external factors, due to the uncertainty in the global macroeconomic and financial environment, global economic and trade growth may continue to be moderate. In addition, the strength of the dollar has led to an increase in the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar, which will suppress Hong Kong's export performance. Regarding local factors, although stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, the drag from rising interest rates is expected to cause private consumption to grow moderately. With the increase in housing supply and the planned development of multiple infrastructure projects, building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily, but a sluggish business climate and rising interest rates will suppress corporate capital expenditure. The government currently forecasts that the Real Gross Domestic Product for 2017 will grow between 2% and 3%, while private sector analysts' forecasts average 2.0%. The prospects for economic growth are constrained by numerous uncertain factors, with the influence from the external environment being particularly significant. The policy uncertainty of the new United States government will make the global economic outlook unclear, and protectionist trade policies that may emerge will bring obstacles to global trade flows. The process of the United Kingdom's withdrawal from the EU and elections in several major European countries may also lead to fluctuations in asset markets and affect the flow of funds in the Hong Kong dollar. Furthermore, the normalization of U.S. interest rates will tighten local currency conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, although local inflation has shown quarterly growth in recent months, the overall trend has remained mild. Year-on-year, the headline Consumer Price Index remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January of this year (Figure 3.4). The basic inflation rate, calculated as the annualized rate over three months reflecting the drivers of inflation, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, and subsequently slightly decreased to 2.4% in January. The main reason for the rise in inflation is the increase in prices of trade goods and housing rent (Figure 3.5). Specifically, the inflation in the prices of trade goods rose to 3.0% in the fourth quarter from the negative figure in the third quarter, mainly driven by the prices of basic food and clothing. At the same time, since the third quarter, with the narrowing decline in residential housing rent and the increase in public housing rent in September 2016, the housing rent component of the consumer price index rose, but subsequently slowed slightly in January (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.4 reflects different indicators of consumption price inflation; Figure 3.5 shows consumer price inflation classified by major components; Figure 3.6 shows the consumer price index for rent items and market rent. In the short term, due to weak import prices and moderate local cost pressure, the expected inflation pressure will remain under control. Due to the strength of the Hong Kong dollar in a certain extent offsetting the impact of the rise in global commodity prices, import inflation will remain low (Figure 3.7). Locally, the output gap in the fourth quarter of 2016 is estimated to remain close to zero, which should help alleviate business cost pressure and thus curb inflation in service-based items. Although the labor market is tight, wage growth has been modest in recent quarters, with per capita real wages rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 and subsequently falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Figure 3.8). Given the continued uncertainty of the external environment, leading to cautious business sentiment, the increase in labor costs should be restrained in this context. Furthermore, due to the poor retail sales performance in recent months, the expected increase in retail property rents will be moderate. Furthermore, the impact of softening private residential rents will gradually be felt, and this will also help alleviate inflation pressure. Overall, it is expected that the annual inflation rate will decrease in 2017, and the government forecasts the basic inflation rate for the full year to be 2.0%, which is low compared to 2.3% in 2016. Figure 3.7 commodity and import prices, Figure 3.8 unit labor costs, and per capita real wages face upward and downward risks regarding the outlook for inflation. Regarding downside risks, if the United States, under the Trump administration, experiences an accelerated rise in inflation, it could lead to the pace of US interest rate hikes being quicker than anticipated, or it may push up local mortgage interest rates, increasing downward pressure on property prices and housing rent. At the same time, an appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar will likely cause import prices to remain weak and simultaneously weaken the local attractiveness for visitors to Hong Kong. Regarding upside risks, if the global economic expansion is faster than expected, it will accelerate the growth of Hong Kong's economic, and push up international commodity prices driven by demand, thereby bringing upward pressure to local inflation. Furthermore, the increased statutory minimum wage will take effect on May 1, 2017, which may lead to further increases in inflation, but the real impact of the inflation driven by this cost will depend on the extent to which labor costs are passed on to consumption prices.

Despite fluctuations in the financial markets, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remains relatively stable, while Hong Kong banks' interbank lending rates are rising along with dollar interbank lending rates. Partly due to the improvement in the local economic environment, overall lending continues to grow moderately. Looking ahead, with the pace of US interest rate normalization accelerating, the unclear policy direction of the new US government, and the geopolitical risks in Europe, volatility in Hong Kong dollar capital flows may increase. Despite fluctuations in the financial markets, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the dollar has remained relatively stable (Figure 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the November US presidential election caused Asian currencies to generally decline, the Hong Kong dollar/dollar spot exchange rate remained stable. However, the interest rate forecasts released by the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on December 13-14, 2016, prompted market expectations for the US to accelerate interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to temporarily weaken thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened in line with other Asian currencies, but due to the rise in market expectations of the US raising interest rates in March from mid-February, the Hong Kong dollar began to show signs of weakening. During the reporting period, no exchange guarantees were triggered (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1 Exchange Rate and Capital Flow Indicator Chart 4.2 The capital flow indicator, following the strength of the dollar, saw the nominal effective exchange rate index for the Hong Kong dollar rise by 4.9% from August to December, and subsequently stabilized in the recent period (Figure 4.3). Due to the minor impact of the narrowing gap in inflation rates between Hong Kong and its trade partners, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar closely follows the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Nominal and real effective exchange rate securities investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016 in Figure 4.3. The latest international balance of payments statistics show a net inflow into local residents' stock and debt securities investments in the third quarter, reflecting an improvement in global market sentiment and a large number of initial public offering activities (Table 4.A). However, the large-scale outflow of debt investment by local residents, driven by the increase in US bond holdings by Hong Kong banks, has overshadowed the investment inflow from non-local residents. Therefore, cross-border securities investment recorded a net outflow in the third quarter. A survey of the global mutual fund revealed that securities investment outflows occurred in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election, coupled with expectations of an accelerated pace of raising interest rates in the US, which pressured local financial markets and other Asian markets (Figure 4.4). However, the latest data shows that the Hong Kong securities investment experienced capital inflow pressure in the first quarter of 2017, partly because investors were optimistic about the US adopting expansionary fiscal policies, which improved the performance of global financial markets. Figure 4.4 Market survey outlook for stock and bond related fund flows: fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. If the pace of interest rate normalization in the US accelerates, it will increase the risk of capital flows to the Hong Kong dollar reversing. At the same time, amid uncertainties regarding the new US government, the UK's Brexit process, and the election of EU member states, capital flows will likely experience increased volatility. Furthermore, the increased investment demand by mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert pressure on the Hong Kong dollar for capital inflow. Although the northbound trading volume exceeded the southbound trading volume in the initial period after the introduction of the Sino-HK Connect in December, it is expected that the bidirectional stock investment capital flow between Mainland China and Hong Kong under this scheme will gradually increase. Despite the rise in dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remains large, and driven by the growth in debt certificates, circulating banknotes, and coins issued by the government, it is expected to rise by an additional 1.7% in the second half of the year (Figure 4.5). In this context, due to the issuance of foreign exchange fund notes amounting to 49 billion Hong Kong dollars to meet the substantial liquidity management needs of the banks, the total reserves contracted, and correspondingly, the outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds increased. Following the market's reassessment of the inflation risk in the United States, global financial markets experienced volatility in the early period. In February, the global market sharply declined from the late end of January highs, completely offsetting the significant gains from the early, and the benchmark 10-year United States Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. Over the past two years, the global market has continued to rise in a low-volatility environment because of market expectations that the economic environment will continue steady growth, and inflation and interest rates will remain low. However, this expectation poses risks of tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionism sentiment, and tense geopolitical situations. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, and the market continues to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall lending continued to increase, but at a slower pace. The increase in property prices and transaction volume recovered in the fourth quarter of 2017 after a moderate slowdown in the previous year. Looking ahead, volatility in global and local financial markets may add fluctuation to capital flows to Hong Kong. Given the uncertainty in the financial markets, and the normalization of United States monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should continue to be vigilant regarding increased interest rate fluctuations and potential capital outflow risks. Especially, given the continuous rise in corporate leverage and the high level of personal debt burden, banks should assess the impact of interest rates increases exceeding expectations on asset quality. After the Chicago options exchange volatility index (VIX) hovered at low levels for more than two years, global financial markets resumed volatility in early. The global market significantly declined from the high point at the late end of January, with the S\&P 500 index falling by over 10%, completely offsetting the significant gains recorded in early January. Market sentiment has shifted, due to indications suggesting that the global economic recovery could put pressure on the long-low United States wages and prices, potentially leading the Federal Reserve to accelerate its interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year United States Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The global market has been on a long-term upward trend over the past two years, based on the expectation that the economic situation will remain favorable. In the second half of 2017, the growth drivers of the global economy continued to strengthen, and economic activities in advanced and emerging market economies simultaneously rebounded. As the year-end approaches, the United States Congress passed a tax reform package, which includes tax cuts and comprehensive reforms to corporate and individual tax regulations, leading the market to anticipate that the United States' robust economic recovery will receive additional cyclical stimulus in the short term. Despite strengthened activities, core inflation in major advanced economies remains mild, further solidifying the market's expectation that global interest rates will remain low for the long term. In this context, the global asset market rose significantly in 2017, with the United States market setting new records repeatedly. However, with the United States releasing January wage growth data stronger than expected, the global market reassessed inflation risk. After short-term fluctuations in the financial markets, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the prospects for the global economy. In the United States, the economy has reached its potential output, and the expected cyclical stimulus from tax cuts may accelerate the inflation rebound, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to hasten monetary policy tightening. Concurrently, as tax cuts will lead to an increase in the fiscal deficit, the United States may issue more government bonds in the future, which is expected to increase upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Federal Reserve continues to pursue balance sheet normalization. Outside the United States, the growth momentum in other major advanced economies is strengthening, leading to market expectations that their central banks may reduce the scale of quantitative easing programs. If implemented, this action will lead to a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from the tense international geopolitical situation could also cast a shadow over the prospects for the global economy's growth. The United States government appears to be increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionism measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of imposing import tariffs on solar panel, washing machine steel, and aluminum. These actions are worrying as to whether their trade partners will respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, once geopolitical tensions unexpectedly escalate, it may affect global trade and exacerbate volatility in the global financial markets. Given the aforementioned uncertainties in the outlook for the global economy, whether the currently high valuations in the global asset market can be sustained is questionable. From a fundamental level, whether the cyclical growth in global demand and the expectation of tax cuts in the United States will lead to an increase in the fiscal deficit and consequently push up the natural interest rates ($R^*$) remains to be observed. The balance sheet normalization by the Federal Reserve will lead to an increase in term premiums or push up long-term interest rates, which is not favorable for asset market valuations. In the Asia-Pacific region, the economies in the area are in an ideal environment of steady growth and mild inflation. With good economic performance and optimistic prospects, capital is also accelerating inflow, and the financial markets are simultaneously rising. However, due to the synchronized normalization of monetary policy by major central banks, global liquidity is tightening. The United States government is implementing inward-oriented trade policies. Tensions in geopolitical situations and the potential for corporate profits to be repatriated to the United States under the revised national tax, which may lead to a large-scale repatriation of profits to the United States, could tighten offshore dollar liquidity, and these factors all expose the aforementioned good prospects to downside risk. Once credit and the financial markets face any shock, a reversal of capital flows is possible, and industries and economies with higher leverage are most susceptible to the impact of tightening financial conditions. In China, the domestic economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by factors such as steady consumption, strong infrastructure investment, and industrial expenditure rebounding near the end of the year. At the same time, signs of the rise of the "new economy" are becoming increasingly evident, with the manufacturing and service industries, among others, exhibiting strong business expansion momentum in the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the economic growth prospects remain positive in the near term, but there are still uncertain factors. In particular, the extent to which the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth from further promoting structural reforms remains to be observed. The mainland authorities announced in 2018 to continue adopting an active fiscal policy stance, which may help alleviate adverse economic changes when necessary. During the review period, progress has been made in both structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. Especially, with the introduction of tightening measures, the domestic real estate market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in first-tier cities. At the same time, due to banks tightening loan approval standards, the risk exposure of corporate entities in overcapacity industries remains controlled by the banks, and shadow banking activities have also slowed down in the context of financial deleveraging. In addition to the positive developments above, our analysis also indicates that the capital allocation efficiency in China, the domestic appears to have improved. Especially, the lending constraints faced by state-owned corporate entities with weaker repayment capabilities appear to have tightened, possibly due to a weakening of the support provided by local governments (see Special Topic 2 on page 28 for details). Regarding external factors, under conditions of stabilizing economic trends and reduced risk, the pressure for capital outflow remained mild for most of the time in 2017. The Hong Kong economy maintained a year-on-year growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real Gross Domestic Product grew by 3.8% in the full year of 2017, the fastest growth in nearly six years. Due to good employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017. Overall investment expenditure also rebounded due to increased corporate capital expenditure. Regarding external factors, benefiting from the improvement in global trade growth, coupled with the gradual recovery of the inbound tourism industry, Hong Kong's export performance has consequently improved further. Nevertheless, because the growth rate of imports is faster than the growth rate of exports, net exports of goods still drag down the growth of the Gross Domestic Product, while net exports of services contribute positively to the growth of the Gross Domestic Product. The economic growth is expected to remain steady in 2018. Private consumption, property and construction activities, and exports will continue to support economic growth. Given that the interest rates in The Hong Kong dollar will ultimately rise, Special Topic 3 will research the impact of higher mortgage repayments on private consumption. The government and market consensus forecast that the growth of the Real Gross Domestic Product in 2018 will be between 3% and 4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, the growth prospects of Hong Kong are still affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, including the economic performance of China, the domestic under tightened financial conditions, the external environment mentioned above, and the trend of the Hong Kong asset market. Although the unemployment rate has fallen to a low of 2.9% in nearly 20 years, local inflation pressure remains under control. However, the pace of inflation has shown a slight increase in the recent months on a year-on-year basis. In this, the prices of trade goods and services have all risen. Looking ahead, the core inflation rate may slightly rise to a still moderate level, partially reflecting the spillover effect brought by the increase in private residential rents. Interbank lending rates in The Hong Kong dollar banks faced upward pressure from September to December 2017. In December, the overnight and three-month average interbank lending rates in Hong Kong banks rose by 14 and 50 basis points, respectively, to 0.25% and 1.26% from six months prior. The momentum of the global economy has remained strong since the latter part of 2016. Improving growth prospects drove the global market to continue rising in early 2017 and early 2018. However, as the market reassessed the inflation risk in the United States, the global market experienced a sell-off and significant volatility in February, marking the end of two years of calm in the financial markets. Looking ahead, tightening global financial conditions, as well as a series of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. In the tight labor market, tax cuts in the United States could accelerate the cyclical rebound of inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to hasten the tightening of monetary policy. As the Federal Reserve continues to promote balance sheet normalization, the United States' issuance of government bonds to finance tax cuts may increase upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The shadow of trade barriers and the potential for an unexpected rise in geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, benefiting from strong export performance and stable domestic demand, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017. However, although the economic outlook is optimistic, it also faces various downside risks, such as the tightening of global monetary conditions potentially exceeding expectations, the United States' inward-looking trade policy, and geopolitical tensions. Once these downside risks occur, the risk of capital flows reversing will also increase. Policy makers face multiple challenges; on one hand, they must guard against the risks facing economic growth, and on the other hand, they must limit the impact of prolonged loose financial conditions on inflation and the vulnerability of the balance sheet. In China, the economic performance in the second half of 2017 was good. During the review period, structural reforms and the containment of systemic risks have made several advancements. Recent growth prospects remain positive, but uncertainties still exist, and this will partly depend on the extent to which rapid growth in the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressure on growth from the further advancement of structural reforms. Due to the stabilization of the economic situation and the reduction of risk, the pressure for capital outflow remained mild for most of 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has been steadily strengthening since late 2016, the growth of economies in advanced and emerging markets accelerated in sync in 2017. Among major advanced economies, investment and exports have steadily increased, driven by the optimistic sentiment in the private sector in the United States and the significant depreciation of the dollar, while the Eurozone and Japan have also recorded a comprehensive cyclical recovery. Exports from emerging markets economies also benefit from the stabilization of global commodity prices and increased import demand from major developed economies. In the short term, following the tax reform in the United States, investment and consumption are expected to be further boosted by the reduction in corporate and individual income taxes. Given the current momentum of cyclical economic upturn and the expansionary effect of the United States tax reform, the International Monetary Fund predicted in January that global economic growth would accelerate from the 2017 estimate of approximately 3.7% to 3.9% in 2018 (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: The forecast for real domestic gross product growth, with the strengthening growth drivers of the Eurozone and Japan, market expectations that global monetary policy divergence will narrow, coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, an increase in stimulus risk appetite and capital inflow into emerging markets economies, will subsequently put downward pressure on the dollar. Despite the Federal Reserve raising interest rates three times during the year and beginning to normalize the balance sheet, the dollar index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite the comprehensive acceleration of economic growth, core inflation in major developed economies remains weak and below their central bank's target, leading the market until recently to anticipate that global interest rates would remain low (Figure 2.2). The expected economic growth in 2018 will remain steady. The economic prospects of Hong Kong are still affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, including the normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, the strengthening of protectionist sentiment in global financial markets, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. In the short term, although local inflation pressure should remain mild, some upside risks still exist. The Hong Kong economy maintained growth momentum in the second half of 2017. The real local gross domestic product, adjusted for seasonal factors, grew by a quarter-on-quarter rate of 0.8% in the third and fourth quarters, which is the same as the average growth rate of 0.9% in the previous two quarters (Figure 3.1). Compared to the first half of the year, private consumption remains steadily growing and continues to be one of the main drivers of local gross domestic product growth. Consumption growth is steady, due to a good employment and income situation, optimistic consumer sentiment, and a positive impact from rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, corporate capital expenditure increased, causing overall investment expenditure to show a significant rise in the last quarter after a relatively stable performance across the three preceding quarters. Regarding external factors, benefiting from the improvement in global trade growth, coupled with the gradual recovery of the inbound tourism industry, Hong Kong's export performance has consequently improved further (Figure 3.2). Nevertheless, due to the faster growth rate of imports compared to exports, net merchandise exports continue to drag down the growth of the local gross domestic product, while net services exports contribute positively to the growth of the local gross domestic product. Given that the Hong Kong dollar interest rate will ultimately rise, this special study examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. Although the improvement in the economic environment will stimulate commercial capital expenditure, interest rates may rise or bring negative impacts. However, the growth prospects of Hong Kong are still affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, including the economic performance of China under tightened financial conditions, the trend of the Hong Kong asset market, and the external environment. Local inflation pressure remained under control in the second half of 2017, but the year-on-year inflation momentum showed a slight uptick in recent months. Year-on-year, the headline Consumer Price Index rose by 1.7% in the third quarter and 1.6% in the fourth quarter, which is similar to the average increase of approximately 1.7% in the first half of that year for consumption. However, the core inflation rate, calculated as the 3-month annualized rate reflecting the drivers of inflation, slightly increased to 2.8% in January 2018 (Figure 3.3). In this, the prices of trade goods and services have all risen. The increase in rent for newly signed private residential properties since mid-2016 may have contributed to inflation to some extent (Figure 3.4). Furthermore, labor cost pressure has remained moderate over the past few quarters (Figure 3.5). Figure 3.3 reflects different indicators of consumption price inflation, Figure 3.4 shows the composite consumer price index, rent items, and market rent, and Figure 3.5 shows unit labor costs and per capita wages. Due to the still mild global inflation and stable local cost increases, the pressure of inflation in Hong Kong is expected to remain mild in 2018, but the core inflation rate may gradually rise from the 1.7% low of 2017. For example, due to the transmission effect brought about by the newly signed rent for private residential properties increase, inflationary pressure may increase in the second half of 2018. Market consensus forecasts the overall inflation rate in 2018 to be a mild 2.2%, while the government forecasts the core inflation rate to be 2.5%. Although the outlook for inflation is mild, upside risks still exist. Regarding external factors, if global inflation or commodity prices record an increase beyond expectations, it may increase local inflation drivers. Regarding local factors, the labor market has tightened further recently, and the unemployment rate, adjusted for seasonal factors, decreased from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, which is the first level below 3% in nearly 20 years (Figure 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be near zero, and if the labor market tightens significantly, it could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Figure 3.6: After the 2008 global financial crisis, interest rates were low, and mortgage debt increased for Hong Kong households. As the normalization of dollar interest rates progresses, the Hong Kong dollar interest rates will ultimately follow the rise in dollar interest rates, and future household mortgage repayment burdens will correspondingly increase, thereby dragging down household consumption. Therefore, this study examines the impact of increased mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. Mortgage repayment burdens refer to the proportion of mortgage debt repayment (i.e., the amount of interest payments plus the principal repayment amount) to the total interest. Figure B3.1 shows the role of mortgage repayment burdens in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. Excluding the substitution effect, income effect, wealth effect, and collateral effect induced by changes in asset prices mentioned in general economic theory, interest rate shocks will also affect private consumption by altering mortgage repayment burdens, subsequently changing household disposable income. This impact will expand with the increase in the outstanding mortgage loan amount. Furthermore, the principal repayment amount will fluctuate with changes in the outstanding mortgage loan amount, which will also affect private consumption by altering household disposable income. Figure B3.1 The determinants of private consumption are measured by assessing the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption; we estimated the outstanding mortgage repayment to total interest ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the mortgage repayment burdens index currently applicable only to new mortgage debt, OMDSR covers the relationship between the total outstanding private consumption and the overall outstanding mortgage debt of households. We roughly reference the standard formula OMDSR used by international settlement banks with fixed installment payments: where Dt is the outstanding residential mortgage loan amount in the banking sector, Yt is the total interest of self-occupied households (measured by multiplying the median total interest of self-occupied households by the number of self-occupied households), and rt and st are the average interest rates and term of the outstanding mortgage loan, respectively. To assess whether OMDSR can reliably measure the entire household's mortgage repayment burdens, it is advisable to compare OMDSR with two commonly used burden indicators. Figure B3.2 shows the OMDSR estimate from 1985 to 2017, as well as the median of the ratio of mortgage contributions and loan repayments to total interest estimated by The government's Statistics Department based on quinquennial population censuses. In the early 2000s, both ratios showed a downward trend, which is consistent with the trend of decreased overall household mortgage borrowing and a significant drop in mortgage interest rates following the bursting of the property market bubble in 1997. Despite the significant rise in property prices following the global financial crisis, these two ratios remained stable due to the monetary authority's macroprudential measures on banks' mortgage lending, which contained overall household mortgage leverage. Furthermore, the extension of the term for new mortgage loans also reduces the actual amount of mortgage payments. Figure B3.2OMDSR and the median of mortgage payments, loans and repayments and total interest ratio; we will also compare OMDSR with the contribution and interest ratio of the banks, the latter being the actual repayment and total interest ratio of new mortgage applicants from the banks. As shown in Figure B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than the ratio of contributions to total interest of the banks, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. Because the original mortgage was established when the property price was lower, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of a new mortgage. Therefore, the indicator for outstanding mortgage repayment burdens covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e., OMDSR) will be lower than the payment burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e., the ratio of mortgage payments to total interest) of the banks. Furthermore, the higher contribution to total interest ratio of the banks is due to the banks complying with the prudential supervision requirements of the monetary authority in calculating the contribution to total interest ratio for both fixed-rate and non-mortgage loans. Following the global financial crisis, the contribution to total interest ratio for OMDSR and banks remained stable, mainly due to the monetary authority's prudent supervision of mortgage loans, which set a ceiling on the contribution to total interest ratio for banks. This measure also helped to stabilize the overall contribution to total interest ratio for OMDSR and new mortgage payments. Overall, OMDSR is largely consistent with common debt burden indicators, but OMDSR has stronger immediacy and can reflect the burden of the total outstanding mortgage debt, and not just the burden of new mortgage loans. Therefore, we believe that using OMDSR can assess the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. To assess the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model according to the methods of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). Among these, the substantive private consumption (measured by the real average private consumption per household) and its long-term relationship with its determinants are presented in the short-term formula as an error-correction term. Based on existing theories and empirical evidence, we consider real income (measured by the median of household total interest, deflated by the composite consumer price index), real housing and financial wealth (measured by residential prices and the Hang Seng Index, deflated by the composite consumer price index) and OMDSR as long-term determinants of private consumption.

Since the Federal Reserve's policy direction depends on the data, financial markets may be more sensitive to future data releases, and monetary policy may become more uncertain. At the same time, as uncertainties in global trade policy and heightened geopolitical risks intensify, they may continue to cast a shadow over the global economy outlook. However, due to the deterioration of the external environment, namely the unresolved US-China trade conflict and the weakening growth of advanced economies, the region may face a comprehensive slowdown. In China, the growth momentum slowed further in the second half of 2018, and the uncertainty of growth prospects increased due to the US-China trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Therefore, policymakers are taking more targeted measures to stabilize the economy and support private and small enterprises. Faced with these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to prevent systemic risks and supporting businesses and the real economy. The monetary policies of other major central banks are also unclear. Regarding the Eurozone, the European central bank ended its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest the full principal of securities that matured under the asset purchase programme, and reiterated its forward guidance to keep the policy interest rate unchanged at least until the summer of 2019. Following these two measures, mainland China also imposed a 25% tariff on equivalent US goods in response. The US further increased tariffs of 10% on imports from mainland China valued at 200 billion dollar imports from mainland China on September 24. Mainland China immediately imposed tariffs of 5 to 10% on US goods in response to the $60 billion worth of US goods. Subsequently, the two countries will engage in negotiations to avoid further imposition of tariffs. Since Hong Kong has always been a transshipment port between these two economies, the imposition of additional tariffs will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the US-China trade dispute has significant implications for the macroeconomic and financial stability of Hong Kong. This study reviews the recent performance of the goods trade in Hong Kong and explores its short-term outlook. We will also attempt to utilize more refined data to distinguish the trade goods directly affected by the imposition of tariffs, in order to more closely examine the impact of the imposed tariffs. To analyze the impact of tariffs, we first extract data for six sets of goods transshipped through Hong Kong, which are affected by the successive rounds of the imposition of tariffs mentioned in the previous section. In the first two rounds of the imposition of tariffs, the US primarily imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-finished products, while mainland China primarily imposed tariffs on agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round of tariffs, the scope of affected goods has expanded, encompassing more consumption goods. For simplicity, the goods affected by the imposition of tariffs in these three rounds will be named List 1, List 2, and List 3. After collecting this more detailed trade data, we will concentrate on analyzing the year-on-year changes in the value of goods transshipped through Hong Kong to adjust for the impact of seasonal factors. Furthermore, readers should also exercise caution when analyzing the data for September 2018, as the trade activities during that month were to some extent disrupted by the super typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the analysis results of this section should only be considered preliminary evidence of the impact of the imposition of tariffs. Shortly after the imposition of tariffs on related goods from mainland China transshipped through Hong Kong to the US from mainland China, the relevant goods appear to have significantly decreased or slowed their growth (Figure B3.1). For example, the growth in transit for List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month after the imposition of tariffs, while the transit for List 3 recorded negative growth. Furthermore, the turnover for all three lists recorded a negative growth in December. The transit volume in List 1 appears to have significantly decreased within a few months after the imposition of tariffs, but has rebounded near the end of the year. The throughput of List 2 was generally in negative growth for the full year, while the growth of List 3 appeared to be relatively stable. In fact, some data and news reports indicate that these early shipment practices are quite common. Some private sector analysts also believe that these actions are part of the reason for the strong overall trade figures pre-tax before the imposition of tariffs. More detailed trade data indicates that certain goods on the tariffs list showed signs of early shipment, but this appears to only involve goods with throughput from mainland China to the US (Figure B3.1). To more fully understand Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine the throughput unaffected by the imposition of tariffs. We found that throughput in the last two months of 2018, unaffected by the imposition of tariffs, recorded negative growth (Figure B3.3). Furthermore, the growth in throughput affected by tariffs (red line) has shown a significantly larger decline starting from the third quarter, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in throughput unaffected by the imposition of tariffs is partly reflecting a weakening of broader external demand. As trade friction continues to lead to increased uncertainties, tightening global financial conditions, and rising geopolitical risks, external demand is likely to be more broadly pressured. Especially trade conflicts have dragged down global economic sentiment and activities, which is reflected in the adjustments of major stock markets. Import demand in other economies is thus dragged down, suppressing the performance of Hong Kong's foreign trade. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting liquidity tightening driven by anticipated seasonal funding demands, which led to the unwinding of interest rate swaps. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar gradually weakened due to funds repatriated by companies from new share capital and the market re-establishing interest rate swap positions, triggering the weak-side exchange guarantee in March. Nevertheless, The Hong Kong dollar transactions remain smooth and orderly. Interbank lending rates in Hong Kong banks generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, subsequently falling in January 2019. Looking ahead, facing uncertain factors such as the ongoing US-China trade friction, the UK Brexit negotiations, and the pace of normalization of US monetary policy, the flow of funds in The Hong Kong dollar may be more volatile. If the Hong Kong-US interest rate differential remains significantly wide, interest arbitrage activities may continue, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for a period in the future and potentially trigger the weak-side exchange guarantee again, which is consistent with the design of the pegged exchange rate system. After the weak-side exchange guarantee was triggered in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the Hong Kong dollar triggered the weak-side exchange guarantee again four times in 2019 (as of March 19) (Figure 4.1). The exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar temporarily rose in September, partly reflecting the tightening of liquidity and the settlement of interest rate swaps, but it gradually declined in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilized again after November, which was due to year-end funding demand driving liquidity tightening, leading to the settlement of interest rate swaps. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partially reflecting corporations repatriating funds from new share capital and the market re-establishing interest rate swaps positions. Due to the widening of the Hong Kong-US interest rate differential after the year-end, it triggered arbitrage activities involving the buying of the dollar and selling of the Hong Kong dollar by market participants, driving the Hong Kong dollar to gradually weaken, and the weak-side exchange guarantee was triggered again in March. Despite the weak-side exchange guarantee being triggered, The Hong Kong dollar transactions continue smoothly and orderly. The total reserve has remained at approximately HK$76 billion The Hong Kong dollar since August (Figure 4.2), and after the weak-side exchange guarantee was triggered in March, it slightly decreased to HK$70.9 billion (as of March 19). The flow of The Hong Kong dollar since April 2018 accounts for only a small portion of the approximately ten trillion Hong Kong dollars that have flowed in since 2008.
