The coronavirus epidemic that broke out in early 2020 simultaneously impacted demand and supply, posing a challenge to the global economy different from previous crises. Although the main central banks and some governments have launched stimulus measures since early November to curb the economic impact of the epidemic, financial markets remain volatile, and the global financial situation has also tightened. Although there are unclear factors in the external and local environments, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and currency market continues to operate smoothly and orderly. Given the stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, stable overall reserves, and moderate growth in total credit, no significant outflow of Hong Kong dollars or the Hong Kong banks system was observed during the period. The total loan amount experienced a moderate rebound in the first half of 2019, followed by a slowdown in growth in the second half of the year. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, but the trend has been somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banks sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the COVID-19 spread situation, future China-US trade relations, tense geopolitical situations, and local social events. Given the continuous increase in corporate leverage and personal debt burden, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolio under conditions where these risk factors may be exacerbated. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, the growth of the global economy has initially shown signs of stability, benefiting from the main central banks' increased monetary easing policies, the easing of US-China trade tensions, and the faded risk of a "no-deal Brexit." However, since late January, the number of COVID-19 infections globally has been continuously increasing, causing market concern and triggering significant fluctuations in the global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks of the epidemic, several main central banks have significantly cut interest rates and increased liquidity tools, while some governments have also introduced measures to support the real economy. However, with the rise in credit spreads and the sharp decline in the stock market, the global financial situation has tightened. Looking ahead, the downside risks to the global economy have increased. The COVID-19 epidemic will impact global economy activities, and the degree of economic impact will depend on the severity and persistence of the epidemic. In the medium term, the relationship between the United States and its main trade partners may become tense again, and trade negotiations with the European Union after the UK's withdrawal may also be very difficult. Weak global demand continues to drag down economic growth in the East Asian region. Exports to major destinations such as the United States, Europe, and China remained weak in the second half of 2019 in the East Asian region. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently announced increased earnings, but whether the technology product cycle will broadly rebound remains to be observed. The financial markets reacted positively to the first phase China-US trade agreement announced in December 2019, and the trade truce reduced some of the uncertainties in global trade. Nevertheless, the East Asian region will continue to face adverse factors such as weak corporate profitability and high private sector leverage ratio. At the same time, the outbreak of COVID-19 has raised concerns that the regional economy may face further pressure amid continued sluggish growth. Travel restrictions implemented by multiple economies in the region may impact the tourism industry in Asia, especially economies that are more dependent on exporting tourism services. Due to the close relationship between the regional supply chain and China, the manufacturing industry may also be affected by the epidemic outbreak. As for China, due to weak domestic and foreign demand, economic growth continued to slow down in the second half of 2019. Looking ahead, although the first phase of the China-US trade agreement helps temporarily reduce the external uncertainties facing the domestic economy, downward pressure still exists in the face of the outbreak of COVID-19, continued economic rebalancing, and the slowdown of the global economy. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 will prioritize economic stability as the focus for 2020 and simultaneously emphasize the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecast indicates that domestic economy economic growth in 2020 will slow to 5.2%. During the review period, domestic authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small private enterprises. Despite relevant measures, some media reports and market analysts point out that private sector industrial enterprises may be facing a decline in shareholder equity in recent years, which is seen as a sign of a "retreat of the private sector." Special Topic 2, through a study of 2018 listed company data on the driving factors of changes in the interests of inland industrial enterprises, found that private enterprises or small enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or "regression." Although research findings indicate negative earnings are the biggest driving factor, other factors, especially structural factors, are also worth noting (see Special Topic 2 for details). Economic activities in Hong Kong significantly contracted in the second half of 2019. Real Gross Domestic Product has continued to decline over the past three quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy has entered a recession. Affected by this drag, the economy contracted by 1.2% in full-year 2019, which was worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and was the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in local demand, especially the reduction in private consumption, is the main factor dragging down the gross domestic product in the second half of 2019. Local social events severely impact consumption activities, leading to a weak economic outlook and subsequently reducing consumer and business confidence. As US-China trade friction intensifies again, the global economy growth slows down, and the Hong Kong tourism industry severely regression, Hong Kong's foreign trade performance continues to languish. Given that the economy is facing significant resistance, the governments introduced multiple rounds of economic stimulus measures from August to December 2019. To allow banks greater room to increase support for the local economy and to help mitigate the economic cycle, the Monetary Authority announced on October 14 that the banks' countercyclical buffer ratio would be lowered from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 to 300 billion Hong Kong dollar to enterprises, especially small enterprises. The economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the recent epidemic has also brought considerable downside risk to the economy. At the end of 2019, global economic activities showed signs of stabilization, leading the market to anticipate a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases has dashed recovery hopes, deepened investors' concerns about a global economic recession, and triggered selling in global financial markets. In response to the economic impact, the central bank and some governments have launched stimulus measures since early November. Given the spread of the epidemic, the downside risks facing the global economic growth prospects have increased. In the East Asia region, the weakening of global demand since the second half of 2019 has cast a shadow over the prospects of the economies within the region. The anticipated coronavirus outbreak is expected to drag down regional economic growth in the short term, with the tourism sector being particularly severely affected. On the other hand, the Asia-Pacific region continues to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage ratio. As for inland China, due to weak domestic and external demand, economic growth continued to slow down in the second half of 2019. Looking ahead, although the first phase of the China-US trade agreement helps temporarily reduce uncertainties in the external factors, facing the impact of the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing, and the slowdown of the global economy, downward pressure still exists, and the authorities' adoption of monetary and fiscal policies to respond will provide some buffer. Under the influence of persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, the manufacturing and investment sectors remained weak, and global economic growth remained sluggish in the second half of 2019. However, economic growth in the final quarter initially showed signs of stability (Figure 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier easing policies of the Federal Reserve and the European central bank, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the initial phase of trade agreements between China-US. However, financial markets still face significant selling pressure, leading to a notable tightening of the global financial situation, which may subsequently exacerbate the downward pressure on the global economy (Figure 2.4). Regarding Europe, the trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to proceed smoothly, which will continue the uncertainties following the UK's withdrawal. Furthermore, oil prices have sharply declined since March, which will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In the East Asia region, due to sluggish global demand, real economic activities in the second half of 2019 remained weak. Exports from the Asia-Pacific region to major destinations such as the United States, Europe economies, and inland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Figure 2.5). Although preliminary signs indicate that the downtrend cycle for local technology products is bottoming out and recovering, including that major local electronics companies have reported an improvement in their 2019 year-end earnings (6), whether exports of local technology products will see a substantive rebound remains to be observed. Figure 2.5: Asia: Weak economic growth and uncertainty in trade regarding goods exports to major destinations continue to trouble investor sentiment, and the total amount of fixed capital investment in most East Asian economies declined in 2019 (Figure 2.6), which may affect potential economic growth in the local area in the long run. To support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea lowered policy interest rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting rates in the first half of 2019, while Thai banks also lowered policy interest rates for the first time since 2015. Figure 2.6 Asia: The total amount of fixed capital formation and the outbreak of the coronavirus lead to concerns that economies in the local area may face further pressure amid continued growth slowdown. Due to multiple economies in the local area imposing entry and exit restrictions on inland China, the tourism sector was hit first, and economies that are more dependent on tourists and tourism service exports from inland China were more affected by this epidemic (Figure 2.7). The ongoing and worsening epidemic will also affect the supply chains closely related to the local and inland China. Figure 2.7 Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese tourists in the short term, this epidemic will continue to affect economic activities and investor sentiment. Referring to the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these impacts may be temporary, but the actual situation will depend on the severity of the epidemic, the extent of its spread, and the effectiveness of the governments' actions to suppress the outbreak. At the same time, economies in Asia also face multiple obstacles. Firstly, although market expectations suggest the company's earnings will deteriorate in the short term (Figure 2.8), the global accommodative monetary conditions encourage yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing asset prices higher without fundamental support. Therefore, the local market is more susceptible to the influence of changes in investor sentiment regarding investment. The expected returns of stocks in the benchmark stock index, Figure 2.8, are secondary, and weak company earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private institutions in the local area to repay debts. Although the decline in local interest rates may provide breathing room for debt-laden companies and households, it may also sow the hidden danger of further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as described in Study 1, when more funds flow into the local financial markets with tracking indices, the risk of debt accumulation for private institutions may also be exacerbated, although this impact may be limited to companies with more stable financial foundations and long-term borrowings. Third, regarding external factors, facing the increasingly stringent trade policies of the United States, the risks faced by East Asian economies may also increase. Although progress has been made in the first phase of the China-US trade agreement, the fundamental issues between the two countries regarding trade still exist, and China-US trade tensions continue. As shown in Figure 2.9, the trade surplus of multiple local economies with the United States is continuously increasing, indicating that multinational companies may continue to seek more supply routes outside of the China-centric supply chain to avoid tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging economies in Asia (excluding China) with the United States has reached approximately $167 billion. If the trade surplus with the United States continues to expand, related economies in Asia may become the next target of the trade war. For example, the United States governments imposed substantial tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In view of this, despite the suspension of trade between China-US, the prospects for local trade remain extremely unclear. Figure 2.9 shows that the trade surplus for the United States over the past decades-high has significantly increased due to the intensification of global cross-border securities investment capital flows by the integration of the international financial markets. A recent study indicates that up to seventy percent of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-tracking funds. 8 Index-tracking funds not only include funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds) but also include funds that actively manage based on investment indices. 9 By introducing overseas investors who were previously unable to attract or access related economies, these funds help to promote the development of the financial markets in emerging economies through investment. Therefore, this type of fund enables emerging economies to achieve investor base diversification for investment, which aids in long-term market growth and stability. However, is there really a free lunch in the world? For passive bond funds, the market is concerned that this type of investment may weaken the fiscal discipline of the issuers of the corporate bonds they invest in, thereby leading to high corporate leverage levels for the companies. Furthermore, some opinion suggests that the growth of index-tracking funds in recent years has exacerbated the volatility of global securities investment capital flows, making emerging economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by other common factors, even more vulnerable. This study assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability. Based on the weight of the bonds within the index in the benchmark index, the passive bond fund allocates its investment funds to the relevant bonds. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds cause the issuers of index bonds to lack the incentive to act from the perspective of fund investors' interests. 13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, this behavior could foster excessive borrowing, bringing significant credit and debt servicing capacity risks to the corporate sector of emerging economies as the leverage ratio sharply increases following the global financial crisis (Figure B1.1). Figure B1.1 estimates the leverage utilization of companies in emerging economies by the weight of those companies within a mainstream index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as the investment of passive bond funds in the bonds of those companies. We find that an increase in this type of investment will raise the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratio of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. Figure B1.2, the blue solid bar represents the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of the emerging market corporate bonds market, the expanded investor base of long-term bond investment due to passive bond funds is also beneficial for the development of companies in emerging economies. We simultaneously found that the aforementioned effects have a significant impact only on emerging economies companies with more robust fundamentals (especially stronger debt-servicing capacity and lower leverage ratio) (green solid bars in Figure B1.2). Faced with higher financial distress costs, companies with high leverage or poor debt-servicing ability do not appear to fall further into debt traps due to investment in passive bond funds. In summary, the above research indicates that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not significantly increase the debt-servicing ability risk in the corporate sector of emerging economies.

Anticipated local inflation pressure will ease, but its outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. The Hong Kong economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On an annual basis, real domestic gross value contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters, respectively (Table 3.A). Affected by the slowdown in the second half of the year's economy, the annual economic contraction was 1.2%, which is worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and is the first annual contraction recorded since the global financial crisis of 2009. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and further climbed to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among them, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors rose to a decades-high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of social events. As the economy's momentum weakened, the overall number of employed persons fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. Among them, the decline in the number of employed persons mainly comes from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction industries. Real wages also decreased by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in response to the aforementioned weak economy's prospects, the labor market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is likely to climb further. Special Topic 3 will explore in greater detail the recent developments and short-term prospects of the labor market. Figure 3.3 Labor market situation local inflation pressure continued to accumulate until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices. Subsequent economic activities weakened, and the inflation impetus also gradually slowed. Compared year-on-year, the headline Consumer Price Index grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, while the growth rate slightly slowed to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The basic inflation rate, calculated on a three-month to annual rate reflecting the inflation impetus, softened from the high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in the inflation impetus is due to a reduction in price pressure on the components of the consumption price index. In terms of trade goods, the rise in pork prices has caused basic food inflation to remain noticeable, although price pressure on consumption goods such as clothing and durable goods remains mild. In terms of services, as the growth in rental components of the consumption price index for residential property has slowed down following the previously signed private residential lease, the growth of the consumption price index rental component also shows a downward trend (Figure 3.5). Labor cost pressure has slightly increased, but has remained at a moderate level in the recent few quarters (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.4 reflects different indicators of consumption price inflation, Figure 3.5 shows the composite consumption price index, rental items, and market rent, Figure 3.6 indicates that the projected local inflation pressure for unit labor costs will ease in the short term. Locally, the weak economic situation and the widening output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential lease continues to slow down, the housing rental items in the inflation should be further eased. In the external sector, due to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices, import inflation is expected to remain moderate. Market consensus forecasts that the overall inflation rate for 2020 will be between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government forecasts the core inflation rate at 2.5% and the overall inflation rate at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is affected by both upward and downward risks factors. On the one hand, given that the estimated output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the severity of the deterioration of the economy is worse than expected (for example, due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic), it may further suppress inflation. On the other hand, if the supply of fresh pork becomes more constrained, it will bring upward pressure to inflation. Although the Hong Kong economy has clearly slowed, the unemployment rate remained at a low of 2.8-2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. As social events continued, the unemployment rate rose to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus pandemic, the labor market will face greater obstacles in 2020. In this context, this study analyzes the recent development and short-term outlook of the labor market, including exploring why the overall labor market was relatively stable in the first three quarters of 2019 (with almost no change in the unemployment rate) and what implications this has for future development. This paper also examines some risks factors that may lead to a sharp increase in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator because some adjustments to labor demand require costs. In fact, the unemployment rate often lags the annual growth rate of the real domestic gross value and the local gross domestic product by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagged nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at approximately 2.9% when economic activities sharply deteriorated in the third quarter of the economy. Figure B3.1: Regarding the real domestic gross value growth rate and the unemployment rate, although the tense China-US trade situation and local social events have dealt a heavy blow to employment in the trade, retail, and tourism-related industries, some key industries are still able to support the overall labor market. Specifically, the number of employed persons in the financial, commercial, public administration, social, and personal service industries continued to grow in 2019, partially offsetting the decline in the number of employed persons in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remains stable, and financial activities in the development of fintech and new share issuance are also very active. These factors may support the employment market in the financial and commercial service industries. Furthermore, public administration, social, and personal service industries, including education, healthcare, and social work activities, appear to have lower sensitivity to the economy cycle. Related coefficient analysis shows that although the number of employed persons in many industries is highly correlated with the real domestic gross value, the response of public administration, social, and personal service industries to the economy cycle is relatively neutral. In other words, even if the economy slows down, the number of employees in these industries may not be significantly affected by the cycle. Figure B3.2 shows the change in the number of employed persons and labor supply in each industries in 2019; the labor force participation rate decreased from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer for the rise in the unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors affecting the change in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bar) exerts downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in the number of employed persons in the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped to suppress the unemployment rate. However, the economy is significantly contracting in the second half of the year, and the decrease in the number of employed people puts upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although the number of employed people decreased during the recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped alleviate the pressure of the rising unemployment rate in the second half of 2019 economy. The factors causing the change in the unemployment rate and some changes in the labor market structure are also worth noting in Figure B3.3. Especially the increase in the proportion of voluntary part-time employees or the ability to retain employees for the company. In fact, the proportion of self-employed individuals and underemployed individuals of the total number of employed people has decreased to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, but the number of voluntary part-time employees continues to rise, becoming the second-largest group of the total working population (approximately 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, the company may retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to approximately 44 hours currently, partly reflecting a greater number of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, the upward momentum was further strengthened in December, and consequently, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained strong within the exchange guarantee range in recent months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar is partly from stock-related demand, and partly due to liquidity tightening near the end of the year which prompted the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar. Overall, the operation of the Hong Kong foreign exchange and currency market continues smoothly and orderly. Although the COVID-19 pandemic in an uncertain external environment may lead to increased volatility in capital flows, Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a stable banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding the pressure of capital outflows without affecting the financial stability of Hong Kong. Supported by increased demand for Hong Kong dollar stock-related assets (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Figure 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar has further strengthened, with the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining in the strong range of the exchange guarantee from mid-December to February. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened, partly due to the robust activities of initial public offerings, and partly due to liquidity tightening near the end of the year which prompted the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar. After the Lunar New Year holiday, the liquidity situation has eased, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has slightly weakened, closing at 7.7956 on February 28th. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued smoothly and orderly during the review period. Since no strong-side or weak-side exchange guarantees were triggered during the review period, the total balance remained unchanged, approximately 54 billion Hong Kong dollar (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Figure 4.2 Summary of balances, foreign exchange fund instruments, and bonds in Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index generally followed the movement of the dollar and slightly increased during the review period (Figure 4.3). Due to the small difference in inflation rates between Hong Kong and its trade partners, the impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar is limited, and the trend of the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar generally follows the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.3 In measuring the flow of funds in Hong Kong, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinct yet interrelated concepts of fund flow: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flow. and (2) cross-border capital flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the monetary aspect of fund flows, which helps assess monetary stability, especially under the linked exchange rate system. On the other hand, cross-border capital flows focus on the movement of fund flows between regions through the Hong Kong banks system, which aids in assess the stability of the overall Hong Kong banking system. Two fund flows concepts require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the total balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, the demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decrease, leading to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Under the linked exchange rate system, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to a weak-side conversion guarantee rate of 7.85 Hong Kong dollars to 1 dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will be prepared at any time to purchase Hong Kong dollars at the request of the banks, and the total reserves will subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the total reserve has remained largely unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been in the strong-side of the strong range of the exchange guarantee in recent months, therefore, there has been no significant fund flows out of the Hong Kong dollar during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, the total amount of credit in Hong Kong banks is a useful indicator. When a large amount of funds flows out of the Hong Kong banks system, bank credit will inevitably decrease. During the review period, the total credit grew at a moderate pace, indicating no significant cross-border capital outflow. The operation of the Hong Kong foreign exchange and currency market continues smoothly and orderly, which indicates that the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Hong Kong monetary environment remains limited. However, we need to closely monitor the risks brought by the COVID-19 pandemic. Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a stable banking system; the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has the capability, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain the stability of the Hong Kong currency and finance. Despite the uncertainty in the external environment and the slowdown in the local economy, the monetary environment in Hong Kong during the review period remained relatively accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar currency base remains substantial, having risen by 4.0% since the late of June to HK$16,894 billion at the end of January 2020 (Figure 4.4). Since no exchange guarantees were triggered during this period, the total balance remained largely unchanged, approximately 54 billion Hong Kong dollar. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds, debt certificates, as well as circulating banknotes and coins issued by the government, are steadily rising. Figure 4.4 During the review period, the broad money supply indicator for the Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained largely stable. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and subsequently increased by 0.2% over the seven months leading up to late June 2019. Due to increased uncertainties in the global and Hong Kong economic environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong saw a slight decline in the second half of 2019. By historical standards, the asset quality remains at a healthy level. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it still grew faster than the credit during the review period. Accordingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratio calculated in all currencies and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio have both increased. However, given that the overall balance of the banks' system is at a stable level and credit is generally remaining stable, the liquidity situation of the banking industry remains sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banks sector of the banking industry will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertain factors such as the COVID-19 spread situation, future US-China trade relations, tense geopolitical situations, and local social events. Given the continuous increase in corporate leverage and personal debt burden, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolio under conditions where these risk factors may be exacerbated. The launch of the novel coronavirus vaccine brings hope for an economic restart, boosting global growth prospects. Coupled with continuous fiscal and monetary easing policies, financial markets have repeatedly reached new highs. However, the global outlook remains shrouded by uncertainties, with the pace of recovery varying across economies. In the medium term, the decoupling of the financial markets from the real economy, high debt levels, and the long-term damage inflicted on the economy by the pandemic will be challenges facing the authorities in the future. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and monetary markets continue to operate smoothly and orderly. The exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar to the dollar is close to the strong currency exchange guarantee level, mainly driven by stock-related demand. During the review period, the total credit increased, with no indication of significant capital outflow from the Hong Kong banks system. Some reflect that the recurring pandemic has led to weakened economic activities and reduced credit demand, with the total loan amount in the banks sector slightly decreasing in the second half of the year, although it still recorded a slight increase when measured for the full year of 2020. Meanwhile, the residential property market is relatively stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties regarding the pace of economic recovery and ongoing geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banks sector. Especially the pandemic will weaken the repayment capacity of enterprises and households, and the banking industry should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 with the resumption of economic activity in various regions, but from the fourth quarter onwards, the rise in the number of novel coronavirus infections caused global growth to slow down again. Nevertheless, with the breakthrough in vaccine research at the end of 2020, market expectations are that the pandemic will ultimately end, benefiting the global economy's return to normalcy and accelerated growth. In addition to the continuous fiscal and monetary easing policies, global financial markets reached a new high in early 2021, although signs of decoupling from the real economy began to felt. In this context, uncertainties will continue to shroud the global economy outlook. The widespread distribution of vaccines is still to be observed. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier accommodative policies could lead to inflation higher than expected, subsequently requiring the central bank to prematurely reduce monetary easing and end the financial markets' expectation of "longer-term low-interest rate" monetary policy. In the long term, decision-makers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures, and address numerous economic legacy issues triggered by the pandemic, including high global debt levels and long-term economic trauma. In the Asia-Pacific region, the improvement in domestic Gross Domestic Product growth in the second half of 2020 was supported by the rebound in export demand. With the increase in risk appetite, securities investment funds in the district are flowing back in, and yield-seeking activities are reappearing. Despite the aforementioned positive developments, the Asia-Pacific region still needs to face the persistent uncertainties brought by the pandemic. Firstly, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, economies with lower development in the district may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service industries. Secondly, the supply, coverage, or effectiveness of vaccines may be variable, coupled with the weakening fiscal situation of the in the district government, which may lead to a deterioration in market sentiment and trigger a reversal of capital flows. As for inland China, with consumption activities gradually recovering to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking at the full year of 2020, the mainland economies grew by 2.3%, being the only major economies to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic prospects still largely depend on the development of the pandemic and the changes in Sino-US relations. The latest consensus forecast indicates that mainland economies will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The RMB experienced several months of depreciation in early 2020, and subsequently strengthened in the remaining time of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the dollar weakened, and strong capital inflows into the domestic bond market occurred. Detailed research shows that during the outbreak of the novel coronavirus, fundamental factors rather than market sentiment played a more significant role in driving the fluctuations of the RMB exchange rate (see Study 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real local gross domestic product remained far below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in local demand and further expansion of goods exports, real local gross domestic product, adjusted for seasonality, began to recover in the third quarter, ending the previous five consecutive quarters of contraction. The annual contraction rate of the real local gross domestic product narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to approximately 3% in the second half of 2020. However, for the full year 2020, the real local gross domestic product fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and this is the first time in history that there has been a consecutive two-year decline after a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest data on local gross domestic product across different industries shows that the contraction in the consumption and tourism-related sectors was worse under the pandemic than the overall economy. The government launched two rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of epidemic prevention and control funds in the second half of 2020 to assist industries and residents affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's epidemic prevention and control capacity. The government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 fiscal budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-time HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and a 100% guaranteed personal preferential loan for the unemployed. The Monetary Authority also, in conjunction with the "coordination mechanism for loans to small and medium-sized enterprises in the banking industry," announced in March 2021 that the "pre-approval for interest-only repayment without principal repayment" scheme would be extended until October of the same year, and announced the extension of the repayment period for trade financing loans under the scheme. It is anticipated that these extension measures will help alleviate some of the working capital difficulties faced by enterprise clients. The novel coronavirus vaccines are expected to enable economic activities to return to normal, with local economy projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (full year total), but the pace and strength of economic recovery are influenced by numerous uncertain factors, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given the time required for widespread vaccines, the local economy still faced significant challenges in the early part of 2021. Regarding external factors, it is anticipated that mainland economies will further strengthened, which can provide support for Hong Kong's goods and services exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccines programs. The government forecasts that the real local gross domestic product will grow between 3.5–5.5% in 2021, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is 4.4%. The labor market situation further deteriorated in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate further climbed to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a high level since the pandemic. In response to the continuously deteriorating labor market situation, the government launched the "Job Retention" scheme under the second round of epidemic prevention and control funds, providing employers with temporary wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to assist them in retaining employees. After the Job Retention scheme ended, the government launched other targeted measures (such as a one-off subsidy) under the third round and the fourth round of epidemic prevention and control funds to further support industries severely affected by the pandemic. In the short term, due to the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Special Topic 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of the Hong Kong tourism industry on the local labor market. Local inflation pressure weakened over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The basic consumption price inflation rate significantly decreased year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third quarter of 2020 and the fourth quarter, and further fell to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February of 2021, respectively. The basic inflation rate, calculated as an annualized rate over three months reflecting the drivers of inflation, has remained at a low level in recent months, despite slight fluctuations. Due to ongoing challenges in the global and local economic conditions, inflation pressure in Hong Kong may remain mild in the short term, particularly as the slowdown in the growth of previously signed private residential rents will continue to curb local inflation. Market consensus forecasts that the overall inflation rate for 2021 will be at a moderate level of 1.4%, while The government forecasts the core and headline inflation rates for 2021 to be 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively. The exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar is close to the strength exchange guarantee level, mainly driven by demand for stock-related funds, including new share issuance activities from Changwang, as well as southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong channels. The fundraising activities during the first two months of 2021 remained active, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain strong. During the review period, the strong party's exchange guarantee was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with funds flowing into The Hong Kong dollar amounting to HK$263.3 billion. The strong party exchange guarantee was triggered 85 times in total for the full year 2020, with a cumulative inflow of 383.5 billion The Hong Kong dollar. Overall, The Hong Kong dollar transactions continue smoothly and orderly. From a regional perspective, during the review period, the total credit increased, and it can be seen that there is no indication of significant capital outflow from the Hong Kong banks system. Despite uncertain factors related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the tensions in Sino-US relations, which may exacerbate fluctuations in capital flows, Hong Kong possesses sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a stable banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding fluctuations in capital flows. With the trigger of the strong party exchange guarantee being activated, the total reserves increased, and interbank lending rates in The Hong Kong dollar banks' industry generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate reflecting the average cost of funds for retail banks in The Hong Kong dollar further decreased from 0.71% at the late of June 2020 to 0.23% at the late of February 2021; due to the reduction in funding costs, the average loan interest rate for new mortgages also decreased from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the most favorable loan interest rates for major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. With the strengthening of the onshore RMB exchange rate, the offshore RMB has appreciated against the dollar since late May 2020. During most of the review period, offshore RMB exchange rates exhibited a premium compared to onshore RMB exchange rates, with the average premium in the fourth quarter approximately 100 points, which is still considered mild according to historical standards. The offshore RMB liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with the total balance of RMB customer credit and deposit certificate balances reaching RMB 826.3 billion as of the late of January 2021. As for other RMB business, loans from Hong Kong banks in RMB decreased, while RMB trade settlements increased, and the daily average transaction volume of the RMB real-time payment settlement system remained at a high level of RMB 1191.5 billion for the full year 2020. Hong Kong possesses efficient financial infrastructure, providing investors with numerous channels for cross-border capital flow to mainland China. With the continued opening of mainland capital accounts, increasing demand for the RMB assets by international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit. Under the support of the rise in the global market and active purchases of Stock through the Hong Kong Stock Connect by investors in mainland China, the Hong Kong market experienced a rebound after a significant adjustment from the beginning of the review period. The global market rose due to major economies adopting unprecedented monetary easing measures. The market is optimistic about the positive progress in vaccine research, believing this may help accelerate the recovery of economic activities. And the unclear factors of global geopolitical have decreased. Against the aforementioned background, the Hang Seng Index recovered its ground after the sharp decline in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period, and briefly broke the 31,000-point level in mid-February 2021, setting a 32-month high. Under stable issuance volume support, the The Hong Kong dollar and offshore RMB bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following a large net outflow of funds in the first half of 2020, as governments in various countries globally introduced unprecedented economic stimulus measures, market confidence quickly recovered, and bond funds flowing into the local market experienced a rebound. Although bond yields have rebounded moderately during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remain near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine research, the market expects the novel coronavirus pandemic to finally be concluded, and the global economy to accelerate its growth thereafter. With the expectation of "longer-term low interest rates" in global monetary policy, investors were not deterred by the pandemic rebound at the end of 2020, and financial markets reached a new high in early 2021. However, the fervent expectations of the financial markets are out of sync with the macroeconomic environment that remains challenging. If the pace of economic recovery is not as ideal, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, due to inflation exceeding expectations), asset prices could experience volatility. Looking to the future, the decision-making authorities will face the challenge of when to withdraw policy support, and how to address numerous issues left by the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-term economic trauma. The continued uncertainty of the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in the East Asian region, and emerging market economies with slower development within the area may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. If the progress of the vaccination program is impeded, it may reverse the current optimistic sentiment, leading to decreased capital inflow and instability in the financial markets. As for China, with consumption activities gradually recovering to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the prospects for economic growth remain uncertain, largely depending on the development of the pandemic and changes in the Sino-US tensions. Therefore, the government has announced the continuation of a supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by the economic reopening, most major economies recorded real Gross Domestic Product growth that was better than expected in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of novel coronavirus infections has risen again, prompting local governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, and the global growth momentum has weakened again. At the end of 2020, a more transmissible variant of the virus felt, which subsequently spread worldwide, making the situation more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine research and the approval of multiple vaccines for use at the end of 2020, market expectations are that the pandemic will ultimately be concluded, and the global economy will return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driver supporting the global economy's recovery comes from continuous policy stimulus measures, including the monetary policy commitment by major central banks for "longer-term low interest rates" amid weak inflation, and the sustained fiscal easing measures by major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus package passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund raised its forecast for global local production value growth to 5.5% in January 2021, an increase of 0.3 percentage points from the forecast made in October 2020 (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1 In the context of the real Gross Domestic Product growth forecasts made by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020, market optimism strengthened, typically benefiting from the rise in stock prices of cyclical industries due to the economic recovery cycle, driving global stock prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Figure 2.2). The 12-month estimated price-to-earnings ratio for major stock indices in Figure 2.2; however, while the financial markets are performing strongly, the macroeconomic environment remains challenging, and the divergence between the two may lead to volatility in asset markets under multiple risks. Although global mechanisms (such as COVAX) promote a fairer distribution of vaccines, the issue of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging economies due to limited vaccine supply is expected to be more severe. Given the increasingly hardline stance of the Democratic and Republican parties in China toward China, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden administration of the government. Should the US-China situation unexpectedly escalate, it may trigger turmoil in the financial markets in the future. Looking ahead, decision-makers will need to face the challenge of whether and when to withdraw epidemic prevention support measures. Although prematurely withdrawing relevant measures could jeopardize economic recovery and cause a "cliff effect," in the long run, the costs of these measures are high, including the fiscal burden and the delay in the necessary reallocation of post-epidemic resources, such as allowing "zombie enterprises" whose business models are no longer viable to continue receiving support from the government. Furthermore, decision-makers must also address the numerous issues left by the pandemic. Firstly, due to declining corporate revenues and increased expenditure by the government, global debt levels rose significantly in 2020 (Figure 2.5). Although the issues arising from the rapid increase in debt due to the current extremely low global interest rates may not be imminent, the continued accumulation of debt by both public and private sectors may cause market concern regarding fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Figure 2.5 The proportion of global debt to the gross domestic product is one issue; the other remaining issue involves the long-term economic losses or lasting trauma that the pandemic may cause. For example, high uncertainty may lead to reduced corporate investment, and workers long troubled by unemployment may permanently exit the labor market, resulting in a significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real gross domestic product recovered in the second half of the year after a sharp decline in the second quarter of 2020 (Figure 2.6). The main driver of economic recovery comes from the rebound in exports, with the demand for exports of electronic and technology equipment being the most eager. Meanwhile, the service industry most severely affected (such as tourism and consumption services that require face-to-face interaction with customers) continues to be in difficulty. Figure 2.6 East Asia: Despite uncertainties in the economic recovery, the inflow of securities investment funds has resumed, even with growth in real Gross Domestic Product in 2020. Since the second half of last year, due to improved market sentiment and higher yields on bonds relative to developed economies, more bond funds have flowed into the region (Figure 2.7). With signs of economic recovery and the launch of vaccine production plans, stock funds also accelerated inflow into the East Asian region in the last quarter of 2020. The currency in the region also appreciated in response to the inflow of securities funds, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Yuan Index to rebound by approximately 10% from its low in March of last year. Figure 2.7 East Asia: Securities investment funds in the East Asian region continue to face persistent uncertainties due to the pandemic. Firstly, although the introduction of vaccines brings hope to the service industry and economy in the region that has been severely affected, competition worldwide for early-batch vaccines has increased procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses a challenge to the region's logistics and public health capacity. Therefore, economies in the region with slower development may achieve herd immunity more slowly than developed economies, and uneven vaccination rates between economies may extend the lockdown period and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Secondly, since investor optimism is largely driven by the introduction of vaccines, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination rates falls far short of expectations, the current capital inflow and the rebound in financial asset prices may cease. A sharp decrease in capital inflow will trigger another wave of market turbulence. With the novel coronavirus successfully controlled and consumption gradually recovering, the domestic economy rapidly recovered in the second half of 2020. Concurrently, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical equipment and high-technology products), exports also maintained growth (Figure 2.8). Looking at 2020, despite the economy encountering unprecedented shocks under the novel coronavirus pandemic, China's domestic gross domestic product still recorded a growth of 2.3%. Figure 2.8: The contribution of each demand component to the growth of the domestic gross domestic product in China Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast predicts that China's domestic economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economy can continue to recover depends to a certain extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in China's have normalized, the service industry is still partially disrupted as the pandemic reappears again in several northern provinces. In the external environment, although exports recovered and grew in the second half of 2020, global demand still exists with uncertainty due to the outbreak of a new wave of the pandemic in most developed economies. Furthermore, the tense situation between the US-China may not ease in the short term, but the previously signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the already achieved China-Europe Comprehensive Investment Agreement can help China and other economies further integrate, or partially offset the adverse effects of US-China decoupling on economic recovery. Considering that the economic outlook remains uncertain, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not undergo major changes in 2021 to support economic growth, while simultaneously emphasizing the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. Furthermore, the latest government work report sets the growth target for 2021 at over 6%. In the long term, the "14th Five-Year Plan" designates self-reliance and strength in technology and dual circulation as priority development directions, aiming for the per capita domestic gross domestic product to reach the level of a middle-income developed country by 2035. Although the real Gross Domestic Product remains significantly lower than pre-pandemic levels, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 with the recovery in local demand and further expansion of goods exports. Anticipating that the vaccination against the novel coronavirus will restore economic activities to normal, the Hong Kong economy is expected to recover growth in 2021 after recording the most severe contraction since 2020. However, the pace and strength of economic recovery are influenced by numerous uncertain factors, such as the development of the epidemic, the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given the time required for widespread vaccine inoculation, the Hong Kong economy still faced significant challenges in early 2021. Therefore, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure in the short term, and domestic inflation pressure remains slight. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activities remained far below pre-epidemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real Gross Domestic Product narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for the full year of 2020, the real Gross Domestic Product fell by 6.1%, the largest decline since record time, and this is the first time in history that there has been a consecutive two-year decline following the 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest data on gross domestic product in various industries also shows that the economic activities of the vast majority of industries have recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with the contraction in the consumption and tourism-related industries being worse than the overall economy. Compared on a quarterly basis, the real gross domestic product began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending a five-quarter decline (Table 3.A and Figure 3.1). Local private consumption recovered to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters, however, under the third and fourth waves of the epidemic, the authorities re-imposed social distancing measures, and consumer confidence remains weak. With the business climate temporarily recovering, overall investment expenditure also increased in the second half of the year. Partially benefiting from the strengthened export performance (especially exports to China), the merchandise trade in Hong Kong further expanded (Figure 3.2). Due to the stagnation of the global tourism industry, service trade remains weak. Overall, the net imports (trade deficit) dragged down the gross domestic product in the second half of the year, partially reflecting the slower pace of goods exports compared to imports. Figure 3.1 Real Gross Domestic Product Growth Rate and Contribution of Major Expenditure Items Figure 3.2 Real Imports and Exports Government launched two rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of epidemic prevention and control funds totaling HK$30.4 billion from September to December 2020 to help affected industries and residents and to enhance Hong Kong's epidemic prevention and control capacity. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 fiscal budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-time HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and a 100% guaranteed personal preferential loan for the unemployed. The Monetary Authority also announced in March 2021 that the "Loan Coordination Mechanism for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises in the Banking Industry" plan would be extended until October of the same year, and announced an extension of the repayment period for trade financing loans under the plan. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate some of the working capital difficulties faced by corporate clients. The novel coronavirus vaccine is expected to enable economic activities to return to normal, with the projection that The Hong Kong economy will resume positive growth in 2021 (for the full year), but the pace and strength of the economic recovery are influenced by numerous uncertain factors, including the development of the epidemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given the time required for widespread vaccine inoculation, the local economy still faced significant challenges in early 2021. Regarding external factors, the mainland economy is expected to further strengthened, which can provide support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccine inoculation programs, thereby affecting Hong Kong's goods trade and tourism. The Government forecasts that the real gross domestic product for the full year 2021 will grow between 3.5–5.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is 4.4%. The labor market situation further deteriorated in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate further climbed to 7.2% in February 2021, a high level in 17 years (Figure 3.3). The unemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a high level after the epidemic. After the total number of employed persons fell to a low point and stabilized (Figure 3.3), the Government figures show that the number of job vacancies continues to decline. The nominal average wage index for employed persons reflecting labor income slowed to a growth rate of 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the continuously deteriorating labor market situation, the Government launched the "Job Security" scheme under the second round of epidemic prevention and control funds, providing employers with temporary wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to assist them in retaining employees. After the "Job Security" program ended, the Government launched other targeted measures (such as a one-off subsidy) under the third and fourth rounds of epidemic prevention and control funds to further support industries severely affected by the epidemic. In the short term, due to the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Special Topic 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of the Hong Kong tourism industry on the local labor market. Figure 3.3 and Figure 3.4 reflect different indicators of consumption price inflation; local inflation pressure weakened continuously over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021 in the labor market situation. The basic consumption price inflation rate significantly decreased year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third quarter of 2020 and the fourth quarter of 2020, and further fell to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February of 2021, respectively (Figure 3.4). The basic inflation rate, calculated as an annualized rate over three months reflecting the drivers of inflation, has remained at a low level in recent months, despite slight fluctuations. Specifically, the price pressure on basic food has eased, and dining out expenses have clearly decreased, reflecting more restaurants offering takeout promotions during periods when dine-in service is restricted. Price pressure on other trade goods (such as durable goods) remains mild. In terms of services, with the stabilization of private residential rents, the rental component of the Consumer Price Index remains weak (Figure 3.5). Labor cost pressure has eased in the recent quarters (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.5 Consumer Price Index for Rent Items and Market Rent Figure 3.6 Unit Labor Cost Due to ongoing challenges in the global and local economy conditions, the pressure of inflation in Hong Kong is expected to remain mild in the short term. Especially affected by the slowdown in the growth of private residential rents previously signed, local inflation will continue to be contained. Market consensus forecasts that the overall inflation rate in 2021 will be at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the Government forecasts the basic inflation rate for 2021 to be 1%, with the overall inflation rate at 1.6%. With the rampant novel coronavirus epidemic, the Hong Kong tourism industry rapidly entered a recession, and the market is concerned that this crisis will have a traumatic effect on the future labor market recovery. Therefore, this special empirical analysis examines the impact of the boom in the Hong Kong tourism industry on the Hong Kong labor market, and explores the potential effects of the current tourism industry recession. Since 2000, the Hong Kong tourism industry has experienced significant ups and downs (Figure B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitors to Hong Kong decreased during the SARS epidemic in 2003. Since the "Personal Travel" plan (free travel) was launched in July of the same year, the number of tourists began to surge. According to the initial free travel plan, mainland residents can apply individually for one to two visits per year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The free travel scheme has been expanded since April 2009, allowing eligible residents holding Shenzhen residency to apply for a one-year multiple-entry "Personal Travel" visa (multiple entries) to Hong Kong. From now on, the number of domestic tourists has significantly increased. Under the promotion of new cross-border infrastructure in travel between Hong Kong and the domestic China, the number of tourists reached a new historical high from the end of 2018 to early 2019. Subsequent local social events caused the number of tourists in the late second half of 2019 to decrease by half, and under the novel coronavirus epidemic, the Hong Kong tourism industry has been stagnant since the end of January 2020. Figure B2.1 Number of tourists and related policies. We will explore the impact of the Hong Kong tourism industry on local employment and income by taking the prosperity of the tourism brought by the free travel scheme as an example. We believe that the free travel scheme launched in 2003 is similar to a random economic shock, because it was almost exogenous in time, and residents of Hong Kong could not have predicted its launch. Our main analytical data comes from population data in the Hong Kong census or mid-term population statistics. Specifically, we use a 5% sample from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016 censuses or mid-term population statistics. Furthermore, we also define the tourism-related industry as the food and beverage, retail, hotel, and transportation industries. First, we adopt the "difference-in-differences" as the analytical framework to compare the differences in employment outcomes between young workers (20-40 years old) in the "treatment group" and older workers (41-65 years old) in the "comparison group" before and after the implementation of the free travel scheme. We will place the younger group in the "treatment group" because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can make significant changes to their employment decisions more flexibly in response to the exogenous growth of the Hong Kong tourism industry. Due to the impact of the boom in the tourism industry brought by the free travel scheme on the labor market being subject to change over time, we also adopt the "event study" method to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical research results indicate that compared to older groups, young workers (especially women and those with only a high school education) are more likely to enter industries related to tourism after the implementation of the free travel scheme. Among these, the free travel scheme has a particularly significant and persistent impact on the probability of young women working in the tourism-related industry, which has remained at a level close to five percentage points since 2006 (compared to the average difference in employment probability for older groups) (Figure B2.2). We also use a similar method to compare the income of the tourism-related industry (treatment group) with the non-tourism-related industry (comparison group). The estimated results show that after the implementation of the free travel scheme, the income growth of workers in the tourism-related industry was higher than that of employees in the non-tourism-related industry. Furthermore, the income growth rate for female workers and low-educated workers employed in the tourism-related industry is higher and shows an upward trend compared to counterparts in other industries (3-20 percentage points) (Figure B2.3). Figure B2.2 The impact of the free travel scheme on female employment, Figure B2.3 The impact of the free travel scheme on the income of female and low-skilled workers. The above results are generally consistent with international experience, revealing that the tourism industry is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women, and low-skilled workers. Regarding the situation in Hong Kong, our research findings are consistent with previous analyses, indicating that the strong growth in the Hong Kong tourism industry has increased the market's demand for low-skilled labor, thereby improving the stability of the low-skilled labor market. As the Hong Kong tourism industry declines to a trough, these labor groups may be more affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continues to close near the forward exchange guarantee level, and the forward exchange guarantee has been triggered multiple times during the period from September to October 2020. Strong demand for The Hong Kong dollar is mainly driven by funding needs related to stocks, including new share issuance activities from Changwang, as well as southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong channels. With total reserves increasing to over HK$450 billion, interbank lending rates among Hong Kong banks have all fallen. Despite uncertain factors related to the development of the novel coronavirus epidemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions between China and the United States, which may exacerbate fluctuations in capital flows, Hong Kong possesses sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a stable banking system, enabling it to withstand the pressure brought by capital flow volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate is close to the forward exchange guarantee level, mainly driven by funding needs related to stocks, including new share issuance activities from Changwang, as well as southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong channels (Figure 4.1). Although some of the funds raised from initial public offerings have been withdrawn, due to the improving sentiment in the Hong Kong Stock market and rising funding demand as the market anticipates the end of the year, the exchange rate of The Hong Kong dollar remained in a narrow fluctuation between 7.7505 and 7.7544 during November and December. With the continued activity of fundraising activities during the first two months of 2021 (Figure 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the dollar closed at 7.7568 on February 26, 2021. Overall, The Hong Kong dollar transactions continue smoothly and orderly. During the review period, the forward exchange guarantee was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the total balance, reflecting a large inflow of The Hong Kong dollar. During September to October 2020, the forward exchange guarantee was triggered 47 times by the strong party. Based on the design of the linked exchange rate system, the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong jointly sold HK$263.3 billion, increasing the total reserves from HK$193.1 billion at late August to HK$457.5 billion at late February (Figure 4.3). The forward exchange guarantee was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with a cumulative inflow of 383.5 billion The Hong Kong dollar by the strong party. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total credit indicates no signs of significant capital outflow from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures show that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any unusual capital flows. Figure 4.1 Exchange rate chart for The Hong Kong dollar Figure 4.2 Stocks raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange Figure 4.3 Summary of balances and foreign exchange fund instruments and bonds during the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index for The Hong Kong dollar generally followed a weaker trend against major currencies and declined (Figure 4.4). As an international financial center, various fundraising activities (such as new share offerings) take place in Hong Kong, resulting in a large inflow and outflow of capital flows to and from Hong Kong. On one hand, the relevant fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, the funds raised by the listed company may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong due to business needs. Hong Kong possesses sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, capable of withstanding fluctuations in capital flows without affecting financial stability. In the situation of continuous inflow of The Hong Kong dollar, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. In the eight months from the late of June 2020, the The Hong Kong dollar currency basis increased by 20.8% (Figure 4.5). By component analysis, the increase in the currency base during this period reflects the increase in the total balance resulting from the forward exchange guarantee being triggered multiple times by the strong party. On the other hand, other components, including debt certificates, government-issued circulating banknotes and coins, and outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds, remain relatively stable. Figure 4.5 During the review period, large new share offerings activities increased the credit in The Hong Kong dollar derived from new share subscriptions, thus the components of the currency base in The Hong Kong dollar (HKD M3) and its credit in The Hong Kong dollar increased significantly during the period from July 2020 to October 2020 and January 2021 (Figure 4.6). Following the conclusion of the new share offerings activities and the repayment of new share subscription loans by customers, the credit in The Hong Kong dollar and broad currency returned to normal levels by the end of 2020. Entering January 2021, the Hong Kong dollar M3 increased significantly again, mainly driven by the large new share offerings activities at the late end of January. Based on the corresponding asset analysis, if the new share subscription loan is excluded, the growth of the Hong Kong dollar M3 is mainly due to the triggering of the forward exchange guarantee driving an increase in the currency base by the strong party (Figure 4.7). As a main component of the Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong credit increased by 22.9% during the same period, and excluding the impact of new share offerings activities at the late of the month, Hong Kong credit grew moderately by 9.1%. Although the decline in the value of The Hong Kong dollar time credit deposits was due to low deposit interest rates, it was entirely offset by the rapid growth in current and savings credit deposits driven by investment demand.
